title: The Odyssey
author: Homer
openingText: Tell me, O muse, of that ingenious hero who travelled far and wide after he had sacked the famous town of Troy. Many cities did he visit, and many were the nations with whose manners and customs he was acquainted; moreover he suffered much by sea while trying to save his own life and bring his men safely home; but do what he might he could not save his men, for they perished through their own sheer folly in eating the cattle of the Sun-god Hyperion; so the god prevented them from ever reaching home. Tell me, too, about all these things, O daughter of Jove, from whatsoever source you may know them. So now all who escaped death in battle or by shipwreck had got safely home except Odysseus, and he, though he was longing to return to his wife and country, was detained by the goddess Calypso, who had got him into a large cave and wanted to marry him.
about:
The Odyssey is the ten-year journey of Odysseus home from the Trojan War. He survives sea monsters, witches, the Cyclops, the underworld, and Calypso's island. He arrives home twenty years after he left to find his palace turned against him: a hundred suitors eating his food and courting his wife by day, his son a stranger to him, his old dog the only soul who recognizes him at the gate. The poem is the homecoming after the war the Iliad described — and the question of whether you can come home at all when you have been gone so long.

Composed orally in Greek around the 8th century BCE and attributed to Homer, the Odyssey is shorter than the Iliad and structured differently: episodic, told partly in flashback, and centered on a single man rather than a ten-year siege. The first four books follow Telemachus searching for news of his father. The next eight are Odysseus's wanderings, told around Calypso's hearth and at a feast in the court of the Phaeacians. The last twelve are the return to Ithaca and the bloody reclamation of his house.

It is the founding adventure story in Western literature, and almost every adventure story since — Sinbad, the Aeneid, Dante's Inferno, Robinson Crusoe, Joyce's Ulysses, Star Wars — is in conversation with it. To read it only as adventure misses the harder argument underneath. The Odyssey is a serious treatment of cunning as a virtue, of what marriage means after twenty years apart, and of the duties a household owes to strangers who arrive unannounced. Odysseus does not come home as a hero who has earned his rest. He comes home disguised as a beggar; he is tested by his own wife; and the violence of his arrival is the price the poem charges for his absence.

angleCards.title: Comfort vs. the journey.
angleCards.text: Odysseus is offered immortality and refuses it. Why does he? And what does it cost him to keep saying no?
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to understand what Odysseus keeps refusing — and why choosing the hard road home over an easy life still matters.

angleCards.title: Greek ethics vs. Christianity.
angleCards.text: Homer's world runs on honor and consequence, not grace. Odysseus kills every suitor when he returns, and it feels right. Understanding why is one of the sharpest contrasts in Western literature.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to understand Greek ethics — a moral world without forgiveness — and what it reveals when contrasted with Christianity.

angleCards.title: Fatherhood and absence.
angleCards.text: The poem opens with Telemachus, who has never known his father. His journey runs parallel to Odysseus's throughout — both looking for the same thing.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow the father-son story — Telemachus growing up without his father, and what happens when they finally meet.

angleCards.title: Intelligence over force.
angleCards.text: Odysseus is not the strongest warrior. He is the one who thinks. Homer's quiet argument — that cunning outlasts brute strength — runs through every episode.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow the argument that intelligence beats force — that cunning is the highest virtue — and see how Homer makes that case.

cast.name: Odysseus
cast.description: King of Ithaca, called polytropos — the man of many turns. Twenty years away from home: ten at Troy, ten trying to get back. He survives by lying, planning, disguising himself, and using words. The poem is named after him and follows him from Calypso's island all the way to a slaughter in his own dining hall.

cast.name: Penelope
cast.description: Twenty years of waiting. For the last three, she has held a hundred suitors at bay in her own house — telling them she will choose a husband when she finishes weaving a shroud for her father-in-law, and unweaving every night what she wove that day. She is the female equivalent of Odysseus: she survives by cunning. When he returns, she tests him too.

cast.name: Telemachus
cast.description: Twenty years old when the poem begins; he has never known his father. He has grown up in a house full of armed men who eat his inheritance and threaten to kill him. The first four books are his — he leaves Ithaca to find news of Odysseus, and the journey is his coming-of-age. By the time his father returns, Telemachus is ready to fight at his side.

cast.name: Athena
cast.description: Odysseus's champion among the gods. She loves him because he thinks. She appears in disguise throughout the poem — as a young man, a shepherd, a beggar — testing those around her and steering events toward his return. She is the patron of cunning intelligence in the Greek world, and the Odyssey is in part her story too.

cast.name: Poseidon
cast.description: The antagonist. Odysseus blinded his son the Cyclops, and Poseidon spends the next ten years trying to drown him for it. The storms, the shipwrecks, the lost crew — most of what stands between Odysseus and home traces back to Poseidon's grudge. The poem opens with the gods debating whether he has paid enough.

cast.name: The Suitors
cast.description: A hundred and eight young aristocrats from Ithaca and the neighboring islands, camped in Odysseus's palace for three years. They eat his food, drink his wine, sleep with his serving women, and compete to marry his wife. The poem makes you know them as individuals before Odysseus kills them, one by one — and that is part of its weight.

whyItMatters.title: The Original Adventure
whyItMatters.body: The Odyssey is the ancestor of every adventure story you have read. Sinbad copies its sea voyages. The Aeneid recasts its hero as a Roman, and Dante uses Odysseus as a final symbol of transgressive curiosity in the Inferno. Joyce wrote a 700-page novel that maps a day in Dublin onto Odysseus's twenty years; you cannot read Ulysses without reading the Odyssey first. Tolkien's hobbits go there and back again. Star Wars borrows the skeleton: a young hero learning who his father is, an older hero returning home transformed, a final reclamation of a usurped throne. The pattern is laid down here — leaving home, encountering the marvelous, surviving impossible obstacles, and returning changed. To read the Odyssey is to read the original of which the rest are variations.

whyItMatters.title: The Hero of Cunning
whyItMatters.body: Where Achilles, the hero of the Iliad, is great because of strength — fastest, strongest, most beautiful, born to die young in battle — Odysseus is great because of intelligence. He is older, smaller, and lies more than any other hero in the Greek canon. He survives the Cyclops by claiming his name is "Nobody." He blinds the monster, escapes by clinging to the underside of a ram, and only as he sails away does he shout his real name across the water and earn Poseidon's twenty-year curse. He passes the Sirens by tying himself to the mast and stopping his crew's ears with wax. He returns home disguised as a beggar so he can study his enemies before he kills them. The poem argues, against the older heroic code it inherited, that survival requires a different kind of greatness from war — and that thinking outlasts force.

whyItMatters.title: Coming Home Is Its Own Trial
whyItMatters.body: The last quarter of the Odyssey is the part most readers do not expect. Odysseus reaches Ithaca around line 13,000 of a 12,000-line poem — and the homecoming is harder than the journey. He cannot simply walk into his palace; a hundred armed men live there now, eating his food, courting his wife, plotting his son's murder. He arrives disguised as a beggar. He tests his old swineherd. He tests his son. He sleeps in his own house unrecognized while the suitors mock him and his wife weeps a few rooms away. Only at the end does he string the bow no other man can string, and only then does the slaughter begin. The poem suggests that homecoming is harder than any of the monsters before it: that returning to where you came from, after twenty years, is itself a kind of monster — and that you have to become a stranger to your own house before you are allowed back into it.
